strengths: Emotion-conditioned image editing is a useful computer vision problem. Generating edits from a source image and a target emotion offers a practical interface for creative applications.

EmoPair provides a substantial resource: 331,595 relabeled InstructPix2Pix pairs and 6,949 additional generated pairs. The manuscript describes the curation pipeline and attributes its underlying datasets and models.

The randomized human preference study provides evidence beyond classifier scores, reporting 56% overall preference for EmoEditor. Qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful changes to emotional cues. The disclosed failure cases and discussion of potential misuse are constructive.
weaknesses: The automatic evaluation is strongly coupled to the method. The same emotion predictor labels training data, filters generated pairs, selects inference outputs, and computes EMR/ESR. Removing iterative selection reduces EMR from 50.20% to 5.06% (Table 1), making it essential to distinguish learned editing ability from optimization against the evaluator. Baselines need equivalent classifier-guided selection and generation budgets, alongside independent evaluation.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. InstructPix2Pix and CLIP-Styler receive single-word prompts that the manuscript already identifies as ineffective. LMS is a useful stronger comparison, but a straightforward emotion-conditioned InstructPix2Pix model trained on the same data is missing. The closely related Affective Image Filter is discussed but not evaluated.

The methodological novelty and reasoning claims are overstated. The global/local branches largely comprise standard emotion conditioning and image-latent conditioning. Because the emotion encoder receives only the target category, it produces eight shared embeddings; aligning these with CLIP instruction embeddings does not establish image-specific symbolic reasoning. Controlled architectural and conditioning ablations are needed to support the claimed mechanisms.

Important mathematical and implementation details are unclear. Section 3.2 defines the noised training latent from the source image and conditions denoising on that same source, without showing how the paired target image enters the diffusion objective. As written, this describes source reconstruction. ESR also places a one-hot distribution in the second KL argument, which ordinarily produces infinite divergence unless smoothing or another convention is specified. These may be correctable specification errors, but they currently hinder verification and reproduction.

Dataset reliability is insufficiently established. Most pairs receive automatic labels from a predictor with 73% accuracy on EmoSet, with no reported independent audit on the synthetic image domain. Confidence filtering alone does not establish annotation validity. Emotion-transition distributions, human agreement on retained pairs, and separate EPAS/EPGS ablations would substantiate the dataset contribution.

The independent human evidence supports a narrower conclusion than consistent superiority. Preference is 54% against LMS online and 49% in the small laboratory study (Fig. S6), with no uncertainty estimates accounting for repeated participants and images. Only 27% of online participants pass screening, warranting clearer retained-sample reporting and sensitivity analysis. Within-valence editing and neutral-image generalization receive only illustrative examples rather than systematic evaluation.

Preserving scene semantics remains inadequately demonstrated. Human participants judge emotional preference without evaluating fidelity to the source, while Grad-CAM-masked pixel differences and edge differences do not establish semantic preservation. Examples replace central subjects, including the acknowledged tiger-to-rocks failure. Moreover, removing either proposed component improves ENRD and ESS in Table 1, contrary to the ablation discussion. The results therefore indicate an emotion–preservation tradeoff that needs explicit measurement and analysis.
